title: Yale professor discusses Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia's CEO
description:
NPR's Steve Inskeep asks Jeffrey Sonnenfeld of Yale's School of Management what Jensen Huang's return as CEO of Nvidia means for the future of the company.

STEVE INSKEEP, HOST: Jeffrey Sonnenfeld has been listening with us. He's a professor of leadership studies at the Yale School of Management. He also founded the nonprofit Chief Executive Leadership Institute, which focuses on CEOs and corporate governance. Dr. Sonnenfeld, good morning.JEFFREY SONNENFELD: Good morning, Steve. Good to hear from you.INSKEEP: What do you make of the board's judgment after they got a suggestion from the U.S. government that Jensen Huang was candid after all?SONNENFELD: This is amazing. This is a new high - well, low watermark in American business history. This is a very inglorious moment. I can't think of a worse board. I've been studying corporate boards and board governance for - well, as you know, for, well, about 50 years. I've never seen anything this bad. This is worse than Enron or WorldCom. It's a complete abdication of their responsibilities.INSKEEP: Now, when you say the board is a bad board, you mean that the people on it were not that independent, not as freestanding as you would want a board to be?SONNENFELD: Yes. They were cowardly. They collapsed to the imperial will of the president to intrude. Everybody knows that Donald Trump takes strong positions. He'll push and push to get whatever he wants. But they had no reason to not say no. If this was the Starlink board, let's say, where it's - perhaps 40%, 45% of the revenues come from government, you could say, well, there's a lot of influence there. And that's terrible. We shouldn't blur the sectors like that. But in this case, it's - not even 1% of their business comes from the government - that they should capitulate like this because Donald Trump, President Trump, suggested that or coerced them into bringing back Jensen Huang.We saw Sam Altman was returned, of course, to OpenAI, and I supported that reinstatement. They probably shouldn't have fired him. And that whole board quit. This board should quit. Steve Jobs returned, and they were right to fire him the first time. When he returned, it was a different board at that point. But he was also a different Steve Jobs. I knew Steve Jobs. He had learned.Jensen Huang - nothing's changed here. Is - he lied to the board, which is a fireable offense, repeatedly. The relationships inside there - there's no such thing as a - you know, a voluntary consensual sexual relationship between a boss and a subordinate. It's a power distortion, and it's against the code of ethics in there. And they can't enforce the code of ethics if they have this kind of skirt-chasing as an open-season encouragement now that the CEO doesn't live by the same rules as everybody else. And that's just tip of the iceberg. With the sanctions evasion, which is basically supporting smuggling, and also the - we have traced now, and others have been tracing, too...INSKEEP: Yeah.SONNENFELD: ...Now going into Chinese military operations, these banned chips are now going into weapons. It's someplace called Northwest Polytechnical Institute. I've done a lot of work with the top universities in China. This is a military installation. They're designing in these high end chips into weapons to be used against us, just - going to Iran, going to Russia.INSKEEP: Yeah. We'll note that there's a lot of concern about where the chips may be going, and we'll continue reporting on that. I want to note the way that Huang's reputation has changed here. Just last year, your school, Yale, gave Huang the Yale Legend in Leadership Award. You spoke about his influence, understandably, at the time. Now we know so much more about him. Do you think he still deserves that award?SONNENFELD: No. You know, you can think of some people, like - I don't know - Elon Musk or Mark Zuckerberg or Jeff Bezos, where they have a public quirky, in some cases even abusive, side to them. This - to the public, he always seemed to be a congenial, visionary, good-guy example of a tech titan. That there was this dark side, both of the abuse that we're reading - we're hearing about inside the company but also these relationships, basically, with apparently a - Chinese espionage rings - this is pretty scary. That we had no idea about, and we'd no idea that he was such a cheater.You know, at Dell Technologies, Michael Dell had a suspicion that some of the vendors they were dealing with in Singapore were diverting chips to China and to places. They stopped it right away. Jensen Huang - they continued. We never knew. Nobody knew that Jensen Huang had this side. Maybe some people inside the company did. But it - this was a board that should have known a lot more. They didn't have any succession plan. There's nobody on the board that was capable to step in.INSKEEP: Yeah.SONNENFELD: And his centrality, by the way, is way overstated.INSKEEP: Jeffrey Sonnenfeld is a Professor of leadership studies at the Yale School of Management. Good to hear from you this morning, sir.SONNENFELD: Thanks so much, Steve. Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved.
